front_blocks.md: Define **xylem**.

back_blocks.md: **Xylem** is the tissue that transports **water** and **mineral ions** from the roots up the plant, and provides **support**.

cards.front_md: Define **xylem**.
cards.back_md: **Xylem** is the tissue that transports **water** and **mineral ions** from the roots up the plant, and provides **support**.

front_blocks.md: Describe the structure of a **xylem vessel element**.

back_blocks.md: It is a **dead, empty** cell with **no cytoplasm** or organelles.
The **end walls** have broken down to form a continuous hollow tube (lumen).
The walls are thickened with **lignin** and contain **pits**.

cards.front_md: Describe the structure of a **xylem vessel element**.
cards.back_md:
It is a **dead, empty** cell with **no cytoplasm** or organelles.

The **end walls** have broken down to form a continuous hollow tube (lumen).

The walls are thickened with **lignin** and contain **pits**.

front_blocks.md: Relate the structure of a **xylem vessel** to its function.

back_blocks.md: **No end walls** and no cytoplasm give an uninterrupted, low-resistance column for **water flow**.
**Lignin** strengthens the walls, giving support and stopping them collapsing under tension.
**Pits** allow water to move sideways between vessels.

cards.front_md: Relate the structure of a **xylem vessel** to its function.
cards.back_md:

**Lignin** strengthens the walls, giving support and stopping them collapsing under tension.

**Pits** allow water to move sideways between vessels.

front_blocks.md: Define **lignin**.

back_blocks.md: **Lignin** is a strong, **waterproof** substance that thickens and strengthens xylem cell walls.

front_blocks.md: What are **pits** and why are they important in xylem vessels?

back_blocks.md: **Pits** are non-lignified gaps in the vessel wall.
They allow water to move **sideways** between neighbouring vessels.

front_blocks.md: Define **phloem**.

back_blocks.md: **Phloem** is the living tissue that transports **assimilates**, such as **sucrose** and **amino acids**, around the plant.

front_blocks.md: Describe the structure of a **sieve tube element**.

back_blocks.md: A **living** cell with **little cytoplasm** and **no nucleus**.
Its **end walls** form perforated **sieve plates**.
The cells are joined end to end into a continuous **tube**.

Its **end walls** form perforated **sieve plates**.

The cells are joined end to end into a continuous **tube**.

back_blocks.md: A **sieve plate** is the perforated **end wall** between sieve tube elements, whose pores allow **sap** to flow through.

front_blocks.md: How is a **companion cell** adapted to its function?

back_blocks.md: It has **dense cytoplasm** and many **mitochondria**.
These provide the **ATP** needed to actively load sucrose into the phloem and to carry out the metabolism of the sieve tube element.

front_blocks.md: Why do **sieve tube elements** need **companion cells**?

back_blocks.md: Sieve tube elements have **no nucleus** and few organelles.
The companion cell carries out the **metabolic functions** that keep the sieve tube element alive and working.

front_blocks.md: How is the structure of a **sieve tube element** related to its function?

back_blocks.md: It has **no nucleus** and only a **thin layer of cytoplasm** around the edge.
This maximises space and reduces friction, allowing **assimilates (sap)** to flow through with little resistance.
